import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1108

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1108](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1108)
-/

open Nat Filter BigOperators

namespace Erdos1108

/--
The set $A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n! : S\subset \mathbb{N}\text{ finite}\right\}$ of all finite
sums of distinct factorials.
-/
def FactorialSums : Set ℕ :=
  {m : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset ℕ, m = ∑ n ∈ S, n.factorial}

/--
A number is powerful if each prime factor appears with exponent at least 2.
-/
def IsPowerful (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → p ∣ n → p ^ 2 ∣ n
/--
For each $k \geq 2$, does the set $A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n! : S\subset \mathbb{N}\text{ finite}\right\}$ of all finite sums of distinct factorials contain only finitely many $k$-th powers?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1108.parts.i : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ k ≥ 2,
    Set.Finite { a | a ∈ FactorialSums ∧ ∃ m : ℕ, m ^ k = a } := by
  sorry

/--
Does the set $A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n! : S\subset \mathbb{N}\text{ finite}\right\}$ of all finite sums of distinct factorials contain only finitely many powerful numbers?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1108.parts.ii :
     answer(sorry) ↔ {a ∈ FactorialSums | IsPowerful a}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos1108

findings.description: The factorial-index convention needs clarification. `S : Finset ℕ` permits selecting both 0 and 1, so it allows the same factorial value 1 twice. Lean proves that 4 = 0! + 1! + 2! belongs to this set but not to the positive-index version. This is not merely a finite boundary difference: for every n ≥ 3, n! + 4 belongs to the current set but not to the positive-index set, whose residues modulo 6 are confined to 0, 1, 2, 3. Both problem statements use this enlarged set. The primary paper supports positive indices, but the website and its linked sequences leave room for the zero-index variant, so I am not treating this as a definite misformalization. Equivalence of the two variants' finiteness claims has not been established.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/1108 defines A using finite S ⊆ ℕ without explicitly resolving whether 0 is an allowed index. Its cited Brindza–Erdős paper, 'On some diophantine problems involving powers and factorials', §1, equation (2), p. 2 (https://doi.org/10.1017/S1446788700033255), uses ∑_{i=1}^∞ ε_i i!, with ε_i ∈ {0,1} and finite support. The linked powerful-number sequence https://oeis.org/A115645/internal explicitly says 'Factorials 0! and 1! are not considered distinct.' Conversely, https://oeis.org/A051761/internal explicitly treats them as distinct and includes 4. The problem's mathematical discussion describes these OEIS entries as including variants.
findings.suggested_fix: If following the primary paper's positive-index formulation, define `{m : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 0 < n) ∧ m = ∑ n ∈ S, n.factorial}`; equivalently, sum `(n + 1).factorial` over a finite set of natural indices. If the current zero-index variant is intended, explicitly identify and source that variant rather than leaving its relationship to the positive-index problem implicit.

reformulations.difference: The formalization includes zero: the empty factorial sum is zero and `IsPowerful 0` holds, whereas powerful numbers are ordinarily restricted to positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For any set A and predicate P on ℕ, let X = {a ∈ A | P a} and X₊ = {a ∈ A | 0 < a ∧ P a}. Then X₊ ⊆ X ⊆ insert 0 X₊, so X is finite exactly when X₊ is finite. This equivalence was proved in the scratch file. Thus this zero convention does not alter the finiteness question, independently of the factorial-index concern.

could_not_verify: Erdos1108.FactorialSums, and consequently its use in Erdos1108.erdos_1108.parts.i and Erdos1108.erdos_1108.parts.ii: I could not retrieve the original Oberwolfach Mathematical Problems, Volume 1 entry [Ob1]. The conflicting index conventions described above prevent a definitive determination of which variant was intended; the remaining aspects of these declarations were verified.
review.notes: Both questions are still recorded OPEN by the source. Brindza–Erdős Theorem 1 bounds the least factorial index for a fixed number of summands; it does not settle either stated finiteness question. Apart from the indexing concern, the quantifiers, k ≥ 2 bound, power predicate, finiteness assertions, and answer scopes match the source. Lean checks also proved `IsPowerful n ↔ Nat.Powerful n` for every n and showed that restricting power bases to positive naturals does not change finiteness. Small subset-sum, square, and powerful-number computations were checked. The completed experiments compile without errors in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and /workspace/review/extra-tests.lean. No repository files were edited.
